name: Jair
interpretive_note: Whether this conquest-era Jair is the same individual as the similarly-named judge "Jair the Gileadite," who ruled the same region generations later and is likewise credited with towns called Havvoth-jair (Judges 10:3-5), is not stated by the text and is debated among commentators -- some read the judge as this Jair's own descendant reclaiming an inherited name, others as a later, unrelated figure who inherited or echoed an already-established place name.
source_summary: A descendant of Manasseh through his mother's line who, during Israel's conquest of the Transjordan, captured towns in Gilead and the region of Argob and renamed them after himself; his territory was still known by his name centuries later, in Solomon's administrative district system.
family_friendly_summary: Jair was a leader from the tribe of Manasseh who helped conquer land called Gilead, east of the Jordan River, before Israel crossed into the promised land under Joshua. He captured towns there and named them Havvoth-jair, meaning "the towns of Jair." Jair's family history was a little unusual -- his father's side of the family actually came from the tribe of Judah, but he was counted as part of Manasseh because of his mother's side, showing how much the land itself mattered to how people were identified back then. Jair's towns were still called by his name hundreds of years later, in the time of King Solomon.
adult_story: Jair, son of Segub, was descended from Hezron of Judah through his great-grandmother, a daughter of Machir, Manasseh's own son and the recognized "father of Gilead" (1 Chronicles 2:21-22). During Israel's conquest of the Transjordan territory, Jair captured a cluster of towns in Gilead and renamed them Havvoth-jair, "the tent-villages of Jair" (Numbers 32:41). Deuteronomy 3:14 credits him with a wider conquest still, taking the whole region of Argob as far as the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites and naming that territory after himself as well. Scripture calls him "the son of Manasseh" (Numbers 32:41) not by direct patrilineal descent -- his father's line traced to Judah -- but seemingly by maternal inheritance and territorial reckoning through Machir (1 Chronicles 2:21-23). His name endured remarkably: centuries later, one of Solomon's twelve administrative districts, centered on Ramoth-gilead, was still described as "the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh" (1 Kings 4:13). A judge who ruled the same region generations afterward also bore the name "Jair the Gileadite" and is likewise credited with Havvoth-jair (Judges 10:3-5) -- whether he was this Jair's own descendant reclaiming an ancestral name, or an unrelated man who inherited an already-old place-name, Scripture does not say.
devotionals: Jair's conquered towns still carried his name centuries later, in Solomon's own records. Jesus's finished work endures forever, never fading with time.
Jair was counted among Manasseh through his mother's line, not his father's -- inheritance by grace, not bloodline alone. Jesus grafts us into God's family the same way.
